title: Χειμὼν καὶ ἔαρ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 346. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Χειμὼν ἔσκωψε εἰς τὸ ἔαρ καὶ αὐτὸ ὠνείδισεν ὅτι εὐθὺς φανέντος ἡσυχίαν ἄγει ἔτι οὐδείς, ἀλλ’ ὁ μέν τις ἐπὶ λειμῶνας καὶ ἄλση γίνεται, ὅτῳ ἄρα φίλον δρέπεσθαι ἀνθέων καὶ κρίνων, ἢ καὶ ῥόδον τι περιαγαγεῖν τε τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ ὄμμασιν, καὶ παραθέσθαι [ἢ] παρὰ τὴν κόμην·
sentences.tr: Cheimōn eskōpse eis to ear kai auto ōneidisen hoti euthys phanentos hēsychian agei eti oudeis, all’ ho men tis epi leimōnas kai alsē ginetai, hotōi ara philon drepesthai antheōn kai krinōn, ē kai rhodon ti periagagein te tois heautou ommasin, kai parathesthai [ē] para tēn komēn·
sentences.l: Winter jeered at Spring and reproached it, that the moment it has appeared no one keeps still any longer, but one man betakes himself to meadows and groves — the man to whom it is dear to pluck of flowers and lilies, or even to carry some rose round before his own eyes and to set it beside his hair;
sentences.i: Winter mocked Spring and reproached it thus: the moment Spring appears, nobody stays quiet any more; one man is off to the meadows and the groves — the man whose pleasure it is to gather flowers and lilies, or to turn a rose about before his eyes and tuck it into his hair;
sentences.n: σκώπτω εἰς is to jeer at a thing; ὀνειδίζω here takes the accusative αὐτό directly, 'reproached it'. φανέντος is a genitive absolute with its subject left out — Spring, which the whole clause is about. δρέπομαι takes the partitive genitive, plucking some of the flowers, not all. [ἢ] is bracketed: Chambry judges an 'or' at that point an interpolation and deletes it, so the English gives it no word. The line is very long and is split here at his ano teleia ·; the ὁ μέν τις opened here is answered by ὁ δέ in the next unit.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ ἐπιβὰς νεὼς καὶ διαβαίνων πέλαγος, ἂν τύχῃ, παρ’ ἄλλους ἤδη ἀνθρώπους ἔρχεται· καὶ ὅτι ἅπαντες ἀνέμων ἢ πολλοῦ ἐξ ὄμβρων ὕδατος ἔχουσι φροντίδα οὐκέτι.
sentences.tr: ho de epibas neōs kai diabainōn pelagos, an tychēi, par’ allous ēdē anthrōpous erchetai· kai hoti hapantes anemōn ē pollou ex ombrōn hydatos echousi phrontida ouketi.
sentences.l: and another, having boarded a ship and crossing the open sea, if it so falls out, goes off now among other men; and that they all no longer have any care for winds or for much water out of the rainstorms.
sentences.i: and another boards a ship and crosses the open sea, if that is how it falls out, and is away among other peoples by now; and none of them gives a thought any more to winds or to the heavy water that comes of rainstorms.
sentences.n: νεώς is the Attic genitive of ναῦς, 'ship'. ἂν τύχῃ, literally 'if it should hit', is the everyday 'as it may happen'. The closing καὶ ὅτι picks up the ὅτι of the reproach at the start: this too is what Winter throws at Spring, so the clause hangs from ὠνείδισεν across the whole length of the sentence. φροντίδα ἔχειν takes the genitive of what one is anxious about, and οὐκέτι is held back to the very end.

sentences.t: « Ἐγώ, ἔφη, ἄρχοντι καὶ αὐτοδεσπότῃ ἔοικα, καὶ οὐδὲ εἰς οὐρανόν, ἀλλὰ κάτω που καὶ εἰς τὴν γῆν ἐπιτάττω βλέπειν καὶ δεδιέναι καὶ τρέμειν καὶ ἀγαπητῶς διημερεύειν ἔστιν ὅτε οἴκοι ἠνάγκασα.
sentences.tr: « Egō, ephē, archonti kai autodespotēi eoika, kai oude eis ouranon, alla katō pou kai eis tēn gēn epitattō blepein kai dedienai kai tremein kai agapētōs diēmereuein estin hote oikoi ēnankasa.
sentences.l: « I, he said, am like a ruler and an absolute master, and I command them to look not even to heaven but somewhere below, to the earth; and I compelled them to be afraid and to tremble and, contentedly, to pass whole days at times at home.
sentences.n: ἔοικα takes the dative of the thing resembled. αὐτοδεσπότης is master in his own right, with no one above him. ἐπιτάττω takes βλέπειν; the three infinitives that follow hang instead from ἠνάγκασα at the end of the line, and in both constructions the men ordered are left unexpressed. ἔστιν ὅτε is a fixed phrase, 'there are times when', so 'sometimes'. The opening « is not closed here: Chambry's guillemets run on to the end of Spring's reply, with the dash marking the change of speaker.

sentences.t: — Τοιγαροῦν, ἔφη τὸ ἔαρ, σοῦ μὲν κἂν ἀπαλλαγεῖεν ἄνθρωποι ἀσμένως· ἐμοῦ δὲ αὐτοῖς καλὸν καὶ αὐτὸ εἶναι δοκεῖ τοὔνομα, καὶ νὴ μὰ Δία γε ὀνομάτων κάλλιστον, ὥστε καὶ ἀπόντος μέμνηνται καὶ φανέντος ἐπαγάλλονται. »
sentences.tr: — Toigaroun, ephē to ear, sou men kan apallageien anthrōpoi asmenōs· emou de autois kalon kai auto einai dokei tounoma, kai nē ma Dia ge onomatōn kalliston, hōste kai apontos memnēntai kai phanentos epagallontai. »
sentences.l: — And so, said Spring, of you men would even gladly be rid; but of me even the name itself seems to them beautiful, and, by Zeus indeed, the most beautiful of names, so that both when I am away they remember me and when I have appeared they take delight in me. »
sentences.i: « And so, » said Spring, « men would be glad enough to be rid of you; but with me even the bare name sounds beautiful to them — the most beautiful of all names, by Zeus — so that they remember me while I am gone and glory in me when I have come. »
sentences.n: The dash is Chambry's mark for the change of speaker; Spring is answering. κἂν is καὶ ἄν — the intensive 'even' with the potential particle, which with the optative ἀπαλλαγεῖεν gives 'would gladly be rid of'; there is no if-clause behind it. ἀπαλλάσσομαι takes the genitive of what one is rid of. τοὔνομα is crasis for τὸ ὄνομα. νὴ μὰ Δία doubles the affirming particle with the swearing one. ἀπόντος and φανέντος are genitives of Spring itself, absent and then appeared. Chambry prints no moral for this fable; Spring's answer is left to do that work.
